history.heading: Kingdoms of the lakes
paragraphs: Uganda, in the African Great Lakes region, was home to powerful kingdoms, including Buganda, Bunyoro, Toro, Ankole and Busoga. Buganda, on the shores of Lake Victoria, became the largest and most centralised by the 19th century, ruled by the kabaka. The Kasubi Tombs of the Buganda kings are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Arab traders, European explorers seeking the source of the Nile, and Christian missionaries arrived in the 19th century. The Uganda Martyrs, young Christian converts killed in 1885–87, are revered.

history.heading: Protectorate and independence
paragraphs: Britain declared a protectorate in 1894, governing partly through the Buganda kingdom. Uganda became independent on 9 October 1962. Prime Minister Milton Obote abolished the kingdoms in 1967.

Idi Amin seized power in 1971 and ruled brutally until 1979, killing hundreds of thousands and expelling the Asian community in 1972. After Tanzania's invasion ousted Amin, Obote returned, and further atrocities occurred. Yoweri Museveni's National Resistance Army took power in 1986. In the north, the Lord's Resistance Army, led by Joseph Kony, waged a brutal insurgency until the mid-2000s. Traditional kingdoms were restored in 1993.

culture.heading: Diversity
paragraphs: Uganda has over 50 ethnic groups; the Baganda are the largest. English and Swahili are official languages, and Luganda is widely spoken. Most people are Christian, with a significant Muslim minority.

Uganda is called the "Pearl of Africa" for its natural beauty, including the source of the White Nile, Lake Victoria and mountain gorillas in Bwindi forest. Matooke (steamed plantains) and the rolex (a chapati with eggs) are popular foods. Runners such as Joshua Cheptegei have won Olympic gold.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Uganda is a presidential republic. Yoweri Museveni has ruled since 1986, and term and age limits were removed. Elections are criticised for repression of the opposition, notably singer-turned-politician Bobi Wine. A 2023 law imposing harsh penalties for homosexuality drew international condemnation. Uganda hosts one of the largest refugee populations in Africa. General elections were held in January 2026.

economy.heading: Agriculture and oil
paragraphs: Agriculture employs most Ugandans, and coffee is the main export, along with gold, fish, tea and flowers. Commercial oil production from fields near Lake Albert, with an export pipeline to Tanzania, is expected to begin around 2026, a project criticised by environmental groups. The economy has grown steadily. The currency is the Ugandan shilling.
